title: The one Giver
hookLine: the Giver alone gives; all others are passing (Sukhmani 14)

lines: THE CHAIN RUNS OUT OF HANDS.
cards: Pick up whatever you ate last. A piece of toast, say. Who gave you that?
The store, sure. But the store got it from a bakery, the bakery from a mill, the mill from a farm. The farmer planted, but didn't make the seed grow, or the rain fall, or the sun rise.
Follow any gift back far enough and the chain of hands gets very long, and then it runs out of hands. Sukhmani has a name for what's at the end of the chain.

teach.b: The stanza that warned against leaning on mortals goes on, in paraphrase: the Giver is the One Lord alone, by whose gift a person is satisfied, and thirst does not come back to cling to them.

That second half is the real point. There are two kinds of giving here. One fills you for a moment and leaves you hungrier: the raise that makes you want a bigger raise, the praise that makes you need more praise.

teach.h: AGHAAI: FULL, AND THE THIRST GONE.
teach.b: The other leaves you satisfied, aghaai, full, the thirst gone. Sukhmani says only the One gives the second kind. The Giver came up much earlier on this path.
In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak asks the Guru for one understanding: there is one Giver of all beings; may I never forget Him. Daataa, in Punjabi, the Giver.
It's an everyday name for God in Sikh speech, thanked in passing when the crops come in, when the baby is born, when the test results are good.

teach.h: EVERY HAND A LINK IN THE CHAIN.
teach.b: Now notice what that does to every other gift. Your boss, your parents, the farmer, the stranger who held the door: they're real, and they deserve real thanks.
But in this picture they're hands in the chain, not the source. Their gifts pass through them.

That's not an insult to them. It's a relief: nobody has to be the bottom of your well. And everything given to you, from the toast to the breath you just took, is a thread you can follow back to the same place.

how: Sikhs call God daataa, the Giver, in daily speech and in Gurbani; Japji Sahib asks never to forget the one Giver of all beings, and Sukhmani's fourteenth ashtpadi names the Giver whose gift satisfies.

o: the Giver, the source of every gift
a wealthy donor to the gurdwara
one who gives alms to the poor

games.q: the one Giver — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza says some gifts leave you thirstier, and the One's gift ends the thirst
by the One's gift a person stays satisfied, and thirst does not cling again.
seeing God as the one Giver means people deserve no thanks
people are real hands in the chain and deserve real thanks; they're just not the source.
daataa is a rare, formal word for God
it's an everyday name for God, in Gurbani and in Sikh speech.

games.q: you just got a raise. a week later you already want a bigger one. what kind of gift was it, in the fourteenth ashtpadi's terms?
o: a gift that ends the thirst.
a gift that leaves the thirst behind.
games.why: a real gift, through real hands, but one that leaves thirst. the stanza says only the One's gift leaves a person satisfied.

practice: Choose one thing you have right now, the water you drank, the clothes you're wearing, the breath in your chest, and trace it back, hand by hand, as far as you can, thanking each hand quietly as you pass it.
When you run out of hands, stop and rest there a moment. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver in whatever words are yours.

wordCard.voice: Daataa, the Giver. Whose gift leaves you full, with the thirst gone; every other giver is a hand in the chain.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daataa, the Giver, a common name for God in Gurbani and Sikh speech.

carryVoice: Your line: one giver. Every other hand is a link in the chain. That's day four hundred ninety-two.
